description: A 9-step branding checklist for startups, plus checklists for launch priorities, brand identity assets, brand guidelines and the brand rollout.
body:
A branding checklist stops a startup from skipping the steps that make a brand hold together: strategy first, then the visual identity, then the rollout.

This is the order I follow on client projects, from seed-stage startups before a raise to established companies after an acquisition.

Below are the 9 steps, followed by four shorter checklists founders ask for most: what to have before launch, the assets a brand identity should include, what brand guidelines must cover, and where to roll the new brand out.

You can also download my branding checklist as a free PDF.

What is a branding checklist?

A branding checklist is a structured guide to the steps and elements needed to build a cohesive brand.

It works as a roadmap for founders, marketers and anyone briefing a designer, so no crucial part of the brand gets missed.

It covers everything from the brand’s core purpose to the tangible assets your team uses every day.

My checklist has nine steps, starting with brand purpose:

  1. Write your purpose statement
  2. Define your core values
  3. Research the industry
  4. Analyse your competition
  5. Create customer profiles
  6. Choose your fonts and colours
  7. Design the logo
  8. Create brand guidelines
  9. Design business templates

What does a startup need before launch?

A seed-stage startup does not need every brand asset on day one, but a few pieces have to be ready before investors, customers and new hires see the company.

ItemBefore launch or a raiseCan wait
Purpose and positioning statementYes
Logo: primary, secondary and icon versionsYes
Colour palette and typographyYes
Short brand guidelinesYesFull guidelines can grow later
Website homepage and key pagesYes
Pitch deck templateYes, if you are raising
Social profiles and email signatureYes
Full template library: letterheads, documents, proposalsAdd as you need them
Merchandise, signage and printOnly with an office, events or physical products
Motion system and brand videoUnless your launch relies on video

That launch set is what I deliver in a one-week Brand Sprint for $3,000, and the website and deck follow at the same weekly rate.

Investors judge the deck and website in minutes, which is why I wrote a separate guide on branding before you raise.

1. Write your purpose statement

Your brand’s purpose statement is the foundation of your whole brand strategy.

It explains why your brand exists beyond making a profit.

Keep it concise and inspiring, and make it reflect the positive impact your brand aims to have on its customers and the world.

A well-crafted purpose statement guides decisions and keeps every brand activity aligned with your goals.

For a startup: write it in one sentence an investor could repeat, and pair it with a positioning statement that names who it is for and what it replaces.

2. Define your core values

Core values are the fundamental beliefs behind your brand’s behaviour and expression.

They represent what your brand stands for and shape its personality.

Values influence everything from company culture to customer interactions, so write them down early.

Make sure they are authentic and memorable, and that they mean something to both your team and your audience.

For a startup: three to five values are enough, as long as each one changes a real decision, such as who you hire or which features you ship.

3. Research the industry

Before you settle your brand identity, understand the industry landscape.

Look for current trends, challenges and opportunities in your sector.

This helps you position the brand and find ways to add value that the market is missing.

It also keeps your identity both relevant and distinctive.

For a startup: collect the websites, decks and logos of ten companies in your category, and note the colours and words they all share, because those are what you need to avoid.

4. Analyse your competition

A competitor analysis shows how other brands in your space position themselves.

Identify their strengths and weaknesses, and look for gaps in the market your brand can fill.

The analysis helps you stand apart and shows which branding strategies already work in your industry.

The goal is not to imitate but to carve out a space that is clearly yours.

For a step-by-step method, see my guide to running a brand audit.

5. Create customer profiles

Detailed customer profiles, or personas, help you shape the brand for the people you want to reach.

Go beyond demographics and focus on psychographics: values, interests, pain points and aspirations.

Knowing your ideal customers in depth lets you write messaging and design an identity that speak directly to their needs.

If you want a quick way to give the brand a personality, start with the twelve brand archetypes.

For a startup: profile the buyer and the user separately if they are different people, and treat investors as a third audience if you are raising.

6. Choose your fonts and colours

Choosing fonts and colours is about communicating your brand’s personality, not only about looks.

Visuals play a key role in how people recognise and judge a brand.

Pick a palette that reflects your brand and appeals to your audience, as I explain in my guide to logo colours.

Choose fonts that are legible and match your brand’s character, whether that is modern, traditional, playful or sophisticated.

For a startup: one primary colour, a few supporting colours and two fonts are plenty, and check that the fonts are licensed for web and app use.

7. Design the logo

Your logo is often the first visual element people associate with your brand.

It should be memorable, versatile and original.

Check how it works across sizes and media, from a favicon and app icon to a billboard.

A well-designed logo communicates your brand’s values and personality at a glance.

For a startup: ask for a primary logo, a simplified secondary version and a standalone icon, each in dark and light versions, and read the types of logos to pick the right style.

8. Create brand guidelines

Brand guidelines, also called a brand style guide, are the rules for using your brand elements.

They keep the brand consistent across every touchpoint, which builds recognition and trust.

Your guidelines should cover your logo, colour palette, typography, imagery style and tone of voice.

They are invaluable for both your internal team and the partners who work with your brand.

The full list of sections is in the brand guidelines checklist below.

9. Design business templates

The final step is a set of business templates that use every element of your brand identity.

These may include business cards, letterheads, email signatures, social media templates and presentation decks.

Ready-made templates keep every communication consistent and professional.

For a startup: start with the templates you use every week, usually the deck, social posts and email signature, and add the rest as you need them.

Brand identity checklist: the assets to have

Use this list to check what a brand identity project actually delivers, or to compare two designers’ quotes.

  • Logo: a primary logo, a secondary or stacked version and a standalone icon.
  • Logo files: SVG, PNG and PDF, in full colour and one colour, for dark and light backgrounds.
  • Colour palette: primary and secondary colours with HEX, RGB and CMYK values.
  • Typography: a primary and a secondary typeface, with licences and the weights to use.
  • Graphic elements: patterns, icons, shapes or illustrations that make the brand recognisable without the logo.
  • Imagery style: rules or examples for photography and illustration.
  • Brand guidelines: one document that explains how to use all of the above.
  • Templates: business cards, an email signature, social media posts and a pitch deck.
  • Logo animation: optional, but useful for video, social and product launches.
  • Source files: editable Figma or Illustrator files, with full ownership after payment.

For what each level of this list costs, see my guide to brand identity cost.

Before you hire anyone to deliver it, go through my questions to ask a brand designer.

Brand guidelines checklist

Good brand guidelines answer the questions your team would otherwise ask the designer.

  • Brand strategy: purpose, positioning, values and personality.
  • Logo usage: versions, clear space, minimum size and what not to do.
  • Colours: values for screen and print, and how much of each colour to use.
  • Typography: fonts, weights, sizes and hierarchy.
  • Graphic elements and imagery: patterns, icons, photography and illustration rules.
  • Tone of voice: how the brand writes, with examples, as in my guide to brand voice.
  • Applications: real examples on the website, deck, social posts and stationery.
  • Files and contacts: where to download assets and who approves new uses.

For real examples, see my roundup of brand guidelines.

Brand implementation checklist

A new brand only works once it replaces the old one everywhere, so plan the rollout before launch day.

Digital: website, favicon, app icons and store listings, product UI, social profiles, email signatures, Google Business Profile and directory listings.

Print: business cards, brochures, proposals and any printed sales material.

Physical: signage, packaging, merchandise, vehicles and event materials.

Legal and admin: trademark filing, contracts, invoices and document templates.

Give each item an owner and a date, and switch everything digital on the same day so customers never see two brands at once.

For a larger rollout, the method in my guide to rebranding after an acquisition scales well.

Brand consistency checklist

Review the brand every few months, because inconsistency creeps in as the team grows.

  • Is the current logo used everywhere, with no old versions left?
  • Do the colours and fonts match the guidelines on the website, deck and social posts?
  • Does new copy sound like the brand voice?
  • Can a new hire find the guidelines and files without asking anyone?
  • Do new products, pages and campaigns still fit the system?

Keep the checklist close

Branding is an ongoing process, but this checklist gives you a solid foundation.

The most successful brands stay flexible and evolve with their customers and the market.

That is why it pays to revisit your brand identity regularly, so it still represents your business and appeals to your audience.

If you want the launch set done in one week, see my Brand Sprint, browse my work or schedule a call.

faq.question: What should a branding checklist include?
faq.answer: Strategy first (purpose, values, industry research, competitors and customer profiles), then the visual identity (fonts, colours and logo), then application: brand guidelines, business templates and a rollout plan for every touchpoint.

faq.question: What branding does a startup need before launch?
faq.answer: A positioning statement, a logo with primary, secondary and icon versions, a colour palette and typography, short brand guidelines, a website homepage, social profiles and, if you are raising, a pitch deck template. Merchandise, print and a full template library can wait.

faq.question: What is included in a brand identity package?
faq.answer: Logo versions and files for dark and light backgrounds, a colour palette with HEX, RGB and CMYK values, typography, graphic elements, an imagery style, brand guidelines, core templates and editable source files with full ownership.

faq.question: What is a brand implementation checklist?
faq.answer: A list of every place the new brand has to replace the old one, grouped into digital, print, physical and legal touchpoints, with an owner and a date for each item.

faq.question: How long does it take to work through a branding checklist?
faq.answer: The strategy and identity steps take one week in a focused brand sprint, or four to six weeks with most freelancers. The rollout adds days or weeks depending on how many touchpoints you have.
